# Introduction

* We study the development of the cfMeDIP-seq,
a platform used to characterize methylation  patterns in 
cell-free DNA extracted from plasma.

* The cfMeDIP-seq assay is the result of optimizing the
low-input MeDIP-seq protocol of Taiwo et. al. (2012) [@Taiwo2012],
which in turn was a specialized version of the protocol
established by Weber et al. (2005) [@Weber:2005aa].

* The sequence data analysis is based on the methods developed for the analysis
of data produced under the regular MeDIP-seq protocol (input > 100 ng).
See Chavez et al. (2010) [@Chavez:2010aa] and Lienhard et al. 2014
[@Lienhard:2014aa]  and Lienhard et al. 2017    [@Lienhard:2017aa] .



<br/>

<p><p/>

<p><p/>
* Wilson et al. 2022 [@Wilson2022]  does not use
sharp metrics or suitable evaluation data to assess the
success of the normalization procedure.                         
   - For model performance, 
*Used held-out spike-ins to assess prediction accuracy*
      - this tells us nothing about the relevant performance -
are the sample normalized methylation profiles better than
the un-normalized methylation profiles.
      - the usefulness of the normalization step can only be judged
by examining the  normalized methylation profiles of samples with
some designed or known truth.

<br/>

* **As a normalization method the spike-in control normalization
remains unproven.**

##     {#FragmentLengthDistribution}

4. Fragment length distribution

* Stutheit-Zhao (2024) [@Stutheit-Zhao2024] show that the 
distribution of fragment lengths adds information to sequence
data when trying to discriminate  between cancer and non-cancer samples.
   - [Rmarkdown](./fragment_length/Stutheit-Zhao_2024_Technical_Review.html)
   - This article contributes more examples of innovative analyses that
are not vetted to any reasonable degree.  There are three methodologies
introduced:
      - 1- Methylation Probability Estimation to get a
Cancer-Specific Methylation (CSM) Score
         - fitting a model with an unmethylated component to a data set which
only targets methylated DNA fragments is an interesting approach.
         - How does it work?  Why does it work?  We are provided no clue.
      - 2- Using reference distribution of fragment length for
normal and cancer populations to obtain a Fragment length score.
         - Using fragment lengths from samples processed on a different
platform is another interesting choice.
      - 3-  The two scores are combined with the weighting determined by 
a logistic regression fit the linear combination of both.
         - the assumption of independent additive effects should be checked.



`r CAPTION <-
paste("Figure 2B from Stutheit-Zhao (2024).",
"  The figure indicates that this fragment length feature",
"adds very little predictive power, if any, to the methylation index.",
"  Recall that this fragment length feature is computed using",
" a reference distribution of fragment length collected",
" using  a different platform."
)`

    
```{r index-fig-2b, fig.cap = CAPTION, include=T, fig.align='center', eval=T}

knitr::include_graphics( "fragment_length/Figure2B.png", dpi=50)

```                   


<br/>
<br/>

<p><p/>
* The analyses have apparent flaws so one should not generalize these
results too broadly, if al all.
   - Fragmentation patterns in cfDNA have proven to be informative
in detecting the presence of cancer in many contexts.  Using a bad
reference may be he problem here.
   - **To Do: a literature review on the ways fragmentation patterns 
can be recorded.**

### Norm Background {-}

* Normalization is one of the steps in the analysis of sample cfMeDIP data
towards cancer detection scores.
* Two models are used, each has the binned coverage as input
   - first model predicts the probability of cancer
   - second model predicts the cancer type
* a 27 fragment spike-in normalization is suggested to adjust coverage levels
   - a scaling factor adjusted for 3 covariates is suggested
   - 4 parameters computed from 27 points which may or may not represent
the sample distribution

* In the task of normalization, we need to counterweigh
the desire to have unbiased estimates with the need to have
low variability estimates.
   - the data need to be examined to see we are on the continuum.
   - a 27 fragment spike-in normalization is going to be on the noisy side

* Alternatively, identify 1000 stably expressed bins and use some one-poarameter
summary of these as shift.

### Study by Study Execution Outline  {-}

#### **Shen et al. (2018) [@Shen2018]** {-}

* Was the Differentially Methylated Regions (DMRs) status between cancer 
and controls used for selecting features?

* CV is to determine the hyper-parameters

```
Training:

* 10-fold cross-validation for hyper-parameter tuning
* Nested cross-validation for performance estimation
* Class imbalance handled by:
   - Weighted loss function
   - Or downsampling of majority class

```
 
* class imbalance is not an issue when comparing algorithms based on the same sample set.

<p><p/>
* auROC is not a good summary
   - spec at fixed sens would be better
   - but both would order algorithms similarly.



<br/>

### Controls, Controls, Controls 

<p><p/>
* Spike-In Controls - Wilson et al. (2022) [@Wilson2022]
   - How are the Synthetic Spike-In Controls used to reduce unwanted variability?


   - Spike-ins may not be affected by some important sources of variability,
but they can only contribute adjustments for variability it is subjected to.
   - What else could be done with these?  
   - What other controls could be exploited? 
      - endogenous controls
      - sample controls

<br/>

### Before any modeling, fitting, etc. 

<p><p/>
* We need to examine the data to get a sense of what the problem is:
   - are there obvious quality issues?
   - are there less obvious quality issues?  
   - visually, how hard of a classification problem  do we have?
      - are cancer types distinct?
      - are there outlier points?  Is the outlier due to technical reasons?
 
<br/>

#### Word on modeling

* It is the error structure in the dataset that dictates the properties 
and validity of the computed statistics 

* Combining data points works well statistically if they are independent with
common mean and variance (+/-)

* statistical modeling is essentially the problem of finding                    contrasts among variables or transformations of variables such that
the contrasts are independent with common mean and sd.

* statistical modeling is essentially the problem of finding                    contrasts among variables or transformations of variables such that
the contrasts are independent with common mean and sd.
